title: Covariance, correlation and direction
summary: SEM estimates are built from how indicators vary together, and because correlation is symmetric the data alone cannot tell you which way an arrow points.

body.text: [[covariance]] measures how two variables vary together, in their own units. [[correlation]] rescales covariance to the range −1 to 1 so it can be compared across variables and studies.

body.explanation: The correlation r of x and y is their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations s. It is unit-free and symmetric: r_xy = r_yx.

body.text: CB-SEM fits the model to the covariance matrix of the indicators; PLS-SEM works with standardised indicators, that is with their correlations. Both therefore inherit a basic limitation: the correlation of X and Y is the same whichever you call the cause.

In a model with only X and Y, the standardised path X → Y equals their correlation. Reverse the arrow to Y → X and you get exactly the same number; only the R² moves from Y to X. Both models reproduce the data equally well: they are [[equivalent-models]] (MacCallum et al. 1993). Direction must come from theory and design.
body.title: Try a wrong model: causal reversal

mistake.title: Taking a good estimate as evidence for direction
mistake.text: A strong, significant path does not show that X causes Y. The reversed model, and many others, fit identically. Claims about direction need a theory, temporal order, or an experiment.

tryIt.task: Run PLS-SEM on this two-construct model and note the X → Y path and the R² of Y. Then select the arrow, reverse it to Y → X, and run again. Compare the two results.

checks.question: In a model with two constructs, you reverse X → Y to Y → X and re-estimate. What happens to the standardised path?

options.feedback: Correct. With one predictor the standardised path is the correlation, which is symmetric. Only the R² moves to the other construct.
Correlation does not depend on which variable is called the predictor, so the sign cannot change.
Unstandardised slopes of y on x and x on y differ, but standardised ones in a two-variable model are both the correlation.

options.text: The reversed model fits worse, which shows the original direction is right.
options.feedback: Both models reproduce the data equally well. Fit cannot choose between equivalent models.

checks.explanation: Equivalent models fit the data identically; direction is an assumption.

checks.question: In one study cov(income in €, satisfaction) = 1200 and r = .30. Another study reports income in US$. Which number can you compare directly?

options.feedback: Covariance depends on the units of both variables; changing currency changes it.
Correlations are comparable across units, though not across populations with very different variances.

checks.explanation: Standardised measures remove units, not every difference between populations.
